strengths: Addresses a clear gap: existing domain-specific code benchmarks lack explicit knowledge corpora, so they cannot evaluate how LLMs acquire and apply new domain knowledge through specialization methods.

Provides a substantial and thoughtfully constructed benchmark: 6 domains, 11 frameworks, 25 projects, 131 core functions, 978 tests, and 107 Q&A items, with multi-granularity requirement descriptions and unit/integration tests.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation includes 10 LLMs, several domain specialization methods (SFT, LoRA, RAG, kNN-LM, code-specific methods), and agentic systems, with additional analyses of contamination, pass@any, sequence length, cost, and errors.

Yields useful and actionable findings: SOTA LLMs struggle on domain code generation; existing specialization methods yield only marginal gains; agents perform best but remain far from solved; cross-domain continual learning causes forgetting; API misuse and data-constraint violations dominate errors.
The benchmark construction pipeline is described in detail, with human review, multi-agent assistance, Docker environments, and explicit ground-truth validation of tests.
Reproducibility is supported by promised release of benchmark, evaluation code, and baselines, plus detailed hyperparameters and experimental setups in the appendix.
The paper takes data contamination seriously, using training cutoff dates and CDD-based contamination detection, reporting low DCI values.
The Q&A task uses verifiable multiple-choice questions, which enables precise evaluation and avoids the unreliability of text-similarity or LLM-judge metrics.
The error analysis and case studies provide concrete insight into why models fail on domain-specific code, especially invalid API calls and data constraint violations.
The work is relevant to LLM evaluation, domain adaptation, and code generation, and could inform future work on retrieval, fine-tuning, and agentic software engineering.
weaknesses: The main code generation evaluation focuses on core function generation, not project-level generation; project-level results are only qualitative in Appendix B. This conflicts with abstract/introduction claims of function-level to project-level evaluation with rigorous test suites.

Domain specialization methods are evaluated primarily with a single base model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct). Conclusions that existing methods yield only marginal improvements may not generalize across base models or scales.

Potential bias: Claude Code or Claude-family models were used during benchmark construction (requirement clarification, test generation, Q&A generation) and are also evaluated as a coding agent. The paper does not sufficiently analyze whether this advantages Claude Code.
No inter-annotator agreement or external validation is reported for the Q&A, requirement descriptions, or test suite creation, making the human quality-control process hard to assess quantitatively.
Statistical rigor is limited: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple-run variance analysis for most main results, despite many comparisons involving small absolute differences.

The RAG domain yields zero Pass@1 for all non-agent models, which is an extreme result. The paper treats this as task difficulty, but it may also indicate ambiguous tasks, insufficient retrieval guidance, or benchmark design issues that need deeper analysis.
The corpus-size analysis in Figure 3 is based on few data points and lacks error bars, yet the paper draws fairly strong conclusions about diminishing returns and method-specific scaling behavior.
Catastrophic forgetting is studied only with SFT in one experimental setup; the broader claim about continual learning across domains is therefore tentative.

The benchmark's notion of "domain knowledge" is largely framework/API knowledge in selected AI/ML software ecosystems, which may limit its generality and relevance to broader computational linguistics or NLP domain adaptation.
Data contamination detection relies on CDD/DCI, which is not definitive, and closed-model training cutoffs are not fully known; the contamination-free claim may be overstated.
The comparison to existing benchmarks may be somewhat unfair because those benchmarks target performance evaluation rather than specialization-method evaluation, even if the distinction is real.

Some claims are overbroad: e.g., "existing domain specialization methods provide only marginal improvements" is supported for the tested methods and base model, but not necessarily for all current specialization methods.
The abstract release URL is missing/blank, and the actual benchmark artifacts are not available for inspection in the submitted manuscript, limiting reproducibility at review time.

strengths: Introduces a novel benchmark that uniquely pairs a curated domain knowledge corpus with evaluation tasks, addressing a real gap in evaluating domain specialization methods rather than only static knowledge.
Construction is thorough: 6 emerging domains, 11 frameworks, 25 projects, multi-level requirements, unit/integration tests, Docker environments, human review, and contamination detection.

Extensive experiments across 10 LLMs, multiple domain specialization methods (SFT, LoRA, RAG, kNN-LM, KNM-LM, DSCC), and agent systems, with additional analyses of corpus scaling, catastrophic forgetting, error types, and cost trade-offs.
Clear organization and rich appendix provide useful diagnostic insights, e.g., API hallucination and data constraint violations as major failure modes.
Timely and relevant to NLP/code LLM evaluation; the benchmark and baselines can drive future work on domain adaptation for software development.
weaknesses: The abstract/title claim evaluation 'from function-level to project-level' is not fully supported: main quantitative results focus on core-function generation, while project-level generation is only qualitatively analyzed in Appendix B.

Contamination control is not fully convincing: some listed frameworks (e.g., TensorRT) do not appear to have been created after March 2024, and the knowledge-corpus DCI is nonzero; models with later training cutoffs may still have seen framework documentation/source code.

The Q&A and test-generation pipeline relies heavily on LLM agents with only human review; no inter-annotator agreement or full human validation is reported, and LLM-filtered questions may bias difficulty and coverage.

The benchmark scale is modest for some tasks (107 Q&A items, 131 core functions), and experiments report single-run Pass@1 without confidence intervals; specialization methods are tested with only one base model and largely default hyperparameters, which may understate their potential.

Agent comparisons are confounded by different base models, tool scaffolding, and token budgets; although control experiments help, the paper does not fully isolate the source of Claude Code's advantage.
Reproducibility may be limited because the abstract's release URL is blank in the provided manuscript, and exact LLM API versions and agent configurations are time-sensitive.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: existing code-generation benchmarks generally lack an explicit knowledge corpus for evaluating domain specialization methods, whereas KoCo-Bench pairs a corpus with evaluation tasks.
Substantial benchmark construction effort: 6 domains, 11 frameworks, 25 projects, 131 core functions, 978 tests, 107 Q&A items, with multi-level requirement descriptions and unit/integration tests.

Broad experimental evaluation: 10 LLMs, standard domain-specialization methods (SFT, LoRA, RAG, kNN-LM), code-specific methods, and coding agents, plus analyses of continual learning, corpus size, error types, contamination, and cost trade-offs.
Includes contamination detection, cutoff-date awareness, and human review in construction, reporting low contamination indices and supporting trustworthiness relative to prior benchmarks.
Error analysis and case studies (e.g., invalid API calls, data-constraint violations) provide useful qualitative insight into why models fail on domain-specific code.
The paper is generally well organized and presents many results in clear tables and figures.
weaknesses: The central claim of multi-granularity evaluation 'from function-level to project-level' is not quantitatively supported: main experiments evaluate only core-function generation, while project-level code generation is analyzed qualitatively in Appendix B. This is a major overclaim relative to the abstract and introduction.

Domain knowledge understanding (Q&A) is only evaluated on 2 of 6 domains (Embodied AI and Ascend Ecosystem), despite the abstract and introduction implying that Q&A spans the benchmark; this weakens the generality of the benchmark claims.

Benchmark construction relies heavily on LLM-generated annotations (requirements, tests, Q&A) with insufficient reporting on human verification, inter-annotator agreement, question difficulty control, or error rates; this raises concerns about data quality and reliability.

The Q&A evaluation protocol is unclear: multiple selections and skipping are allowed, but the accuracy metric is not defined for partial selections, skipped questions, or multiple correct answers, making the reported ACC difficult to interpret.

Claude Code is used during benchmark construction and is also the best-performing evaluated agent, creating a possible circularity/bias; the paper does not analyze whether construction artifacts disproportionately favor Claude Code.

The domain-specialization baselines are standard but potentially weak: SFT/LoRA train on randomly concatenated corpus chunks for 5 epochs with no validation or per-domain tuning, and average Pass@1 does not improve over the base model. The conclusion that methods yield 'marginal improvements' is therefore generous and may partly reflect implementation choices.

Reproducibility is limited by missing details: the release URL is absent in the review version, and the paper omits data splits, project/framework licensing, annotator qualifications/compensation, and exact filtering criteria for Q&A.
The corpus-size analysis in Figure 3 is difficult to interpret: x-axis values are not sorted, only four points are shown, and the correlation claims are not robustly supported.
The Limitations section is incomplete, focusing on contamination and missing newer models while ignoring the project-level evaluation gap, limited Q&A domain coverage, and construction-bias concerns.
